title: Comments and Readable C Source Code
learningObjectives: Explain how `//` line comments and `/* ... */` block comments are recognized in C source.
Distinguish comment markers from identical characters appearing inside string and character literals.
Document intent, assumptions, units, invariants and non-obvious decisions with concise comments.
Recognize that standard C block comments do not nest and avoid accidentally commenting out code.
Keep comments accurate and never place credentials or other secrets in source comments.

understand.concept: Comments are explanatory text in source code that the compiler does not treat as executable C tokens. C supports single-line comments beginning with // and block comments beginning with /* and ending with */. Comments should explain intent, assumptions, constraints and non-obvious decisions rather than repeat what each line visibly does.
understand.whyItMatters: Readable source code reduces maintenance cost and helps another developer understand why a decision was made. Good comments preserve context that names and code structure alone may not communicate.
understand.analogy: Think of a C program as a set of precise instructions that must be translated for a particular machine and execution environment.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace the formal C language rules, object lifetimes, types or implementation-defined behaviour.

explain.narrative:
A single-line comment begins with // and continues to the end of the source line. A block comment begins with /* and ends at the next */; standard C block comments do not nest. A comment marker inside a string literal is ordinary string content, not the beginning of a comment.

Comments can document a function's contract, explain a boundary condition, record units, state ownership expectations or clarify a workaround. They become harmful when they are stale, inaccurate or merely restate obvious code. Keep comments close to the code they explain and update them when behaviour changes.

Do not store passwords, API keys, personal information or other secrets in comments. Comments remain in source repositories and may be included in distributed source packages. Removing a comment from a compiled executable does not make a secret safe if it was also embedded in program data.

examples.title: Single-line and block comments in a complete program
examples.explanation: The comments document intent and an assumption that affects how the code should be understood. The complete program prints 2 hours and 15 minutes.

examples.title: Comment markers inside a string literal
examples.explanation: The // characters are part of the string literal; they do not begin a source-code comment. This complete program prints the text unchanged.

practise.guidedTask: Add comments to a small conversion program. Explain its input assumptions, units and one non-obvious decision. Remove comments that only repeat the next statement.
practise.independentTask: Review a short program with misleading and outdated comments. Rewrite the comments to match actual behaviour, document one precondition and remove any secret-like value from the source.
hints: // comments continue to the end of the line.
/* ... */ comments end at the first closing delimiter and do not nest in standard C.
Comment markers inside string literals are ordinary characters.
Document intent, assumptions and contracts instead of narrating every obvious line.
Never put credentials or private data in comments or source control.

questions.prompt: Which token begins a C single-line comment?
questions.explanation: A `//` comment continues to the end of the source line.

questions.prompt: How does a C block comment end?
questions.explanation: A block comment begins with `/*` and ends at the next `*/`.

questions.prompt: What happens to `//` inside the string literal `"https://example.com"`?
options: It is ordinary string content, not a comment opener
It starts a comment inside the string
It causes the string to end
questions.answer: It is ordinary string content, not a comment opener
questions.explanation: Comment delimiters are not recognized as comments while they are part of a string literal.

questions.prompt: Which comment is most useful in maintainable code?
options: One explaining a non-obvious constraint or reason
One repeating every assignment in plain English
questions.answer: One explaining a non-obvious constraint or reason
questions.explanation: Comments should add context that is not already obvious from the code.

questions.prompt: Can standard C block comments be nested?
questions.explanation: The first `*/` ends a standard C block comment, so nested-looking comments can terminate unexpectedly.
